══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n# Per-model basin agreement (do individual models agree on basin geometry?)\n# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n\ndef analyze_per_model_basins(\n    consensus_results: dict[float, dict],\n    probes: list[dict],\n    target_frac: float = 0.5,\n) -> dict:\n    \"\"\"Check if individual models agree on basin geometry at a given depth.\n\n    For each domain, extract the domain→combinator fingerprint from\n    EACH model separately, then measure cross-model agreement on\n    that fingerprint.\n    \"\"\"\n    domain_indices = get_domain_indices(probes)\n    pure_indices = get_pure_indices(probes)\n\n    if target_frac not in consensus_results:\n        # Find closest\n        fracs = sorted(consensus_results.keys())\n        target_frac = min(fracs, key=lambda f: abs(f - target_frac))\n\n    result = consensus_results[target_frac]\n    stacked = result[\"stacked_rdms\"]  # (n_models, n_probes, n_probes)\n    n_models = stacked.shape[0]\n    model_keys = result[\"stats\"][\"model_keys\"]\n\n    per_model_results = {}\n\n    for domain in SKILL_DOMAINS:\n        if domain not in domain_indices:\n            continue\n\n        d_idx = domain_indices[domain]\n\n        # Extract fingerprint from each model\n        model_fingerprints = []\n        for mi in range(n_models):\n            rdm_i = stacked[mi]\n            fp = []\n            for comb in COMBINATOR_ORDER:\n                if comb not in pure_indices:\n                    fp.append(0.0)\n                    continue\n                ci = pure_indices[comb]\n                sims = [float(rdm_i[di, ci]) for di in d_idx]\n                fp.append(float(np.mean(sims)))\n            model_fingerprints.append(np.array(fp))\n\n        # Cross-model correlation on fingerprints\n        correlations = []\n        for i in range(n_models):\n            for j in range(i + 1, n_models):\n                corr = np.corrcoef(model_fingerprints[i], model_fingerprints[j])[0, 1]\n                correlations.append(float(corr))\n\n        # Cross-model agreement on dominant combinator\n        dominants = [COMBINATOR_ORDER[np.argmax(fp)] for fp in model_fingerprints]\n        dominant_agreement = len(set(dominants)) == 1\n\n        per_model_results[domain] = {\n            \"model_fingerprints\": {\n                mk: {c: float(fp[ci]) for ci, c in enumerate(COMBINATOR_ORDER)}\n                for mk, fp in zip(model_keys, model_fingerprints)\n            },\n            \"cross_model_correlation\": float(np.mean(correlations)) if correlations else 0.0,\n            \"per_pair_correlation\": correlations,\n            \"dominant_per_model\": dict(zip(model_keys, dominants)),\n            \"dominant_unanimous\": dominant_agreement,\n            \"consensus_dominant\": max(\n                COMBINATOR_ORDER,\n                key=lambda c: float(np.mean([fp[COMBINATOR_ORDER.index(c)]\n                                             for fp in model_fingerprints]))\n            ),\n        }\n\n    return {\n        \"depth_fraction\": target_frac,\n        \"n_models\": n_models,\n        \"model_keys\": model_keys,\n        \"domains\": per_model_results,\n    }\n\n\n# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n# Pretty printing\n# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n\ndef print_basin_analysis(analysis: dict, per_model: dict) -> None:\n    \"\"\"Print human-readable basin analysis.\"\"\"\n    print(\"\\n\" + \"=\" * 90, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"  CRYSTAL BASIN ANALYSIS — Multi-Domain Skill Attractors\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"=\" * 90, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    # ── Domain fingerprints at mid-depth ──────────────────────\n    mid_key = None\n    for fk in analysis[\"depth_fractions\"]:\n        if abs(fk - 0.5) < 0.1:\n            mid_key = f\"{fk:.2f}\"\n            break\n    if not mid_key:\n        mid_key = f\"{analysis['depth_fractions'][len(analysis['depth_fractions'])//2]:.2f}\"\n\n    print(f\"\\n  Domain → Combinator Fingerprints (depth {mid_key}):\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(f\"  {'domain':>12s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n    for c in COMBINATOR_ORDER:\n        print(f\"  {c:>6s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n    print(f\"  {'dom':>5s}  {'coher':>6s}  {'agree':>6s}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"  \" + \"-\" * 100, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    for domain in SKILL_DOMAINS:\n        if domain not in analysis[\"per_domain\"]:\n            continue\n        geo = analysis[\"per_domain\"][domain].get(mid_key)\n        if not geo:\n            continue\n        print(f\"  {domain:>12s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        for c in COMBINATOR_ORDER:\n            sim = geo[\"fingerprint\"].get(c, {}).get(\"mean_sim\", 0)\n            print(f\"  {sim:+.3f}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        print(f\"  {geo['dominant_combinator']:>5s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        print(f\"  {geo['internal_coherence']:+.3f}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        print(f\"  {geo['internal_agreement']:.3f}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    # ── Cross-domain fingerprint similarity ───────────────────\n    cross = analysis[\"cross_domain\"].get(mid_key)\n    if cross:\n        print(f\"\\n  Cross-Domain Fingerprint Similarity (depth {mid_key}):\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n        domains = cross[\"domains\"]\n        fp_sim = np.array(cross[\"fingerprint_similarity\"])\n\n        print(f\"  {'':>12s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        for d in domains:\n            print(f\"  {d[:6]:>6s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        print(file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n        for i, di in enumerate(domains):\n            print(f\"  {di:>12s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n            for j, dj in enumerate(domains):\n                if i == j:\n                    print(f\"  {'--':>6s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n                else:\n                    print(f\"  {fp_sim[i,j]:+.3f}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n            print(file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    # ── Basin summary ─────────────────────────────────────────\n    print(f\"\\n  Basin Summary Across Depths:\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(f\"  {'depth':>6s}  {'mean_fp_sim':>11s}  {'min_fp_sim':>10s}  \"\n          f\"{'max_fp_sim':>10s}  {'mean_agree':>10s}\",\n          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"  \" + \"-\" * 56, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    for frac_key in sorted(analysis[\"basin_summary\"].keys()):\n        bs = analysis[\"basin_summary\"][frac_key]\n        print(f\"  {frac_key:>6s}  {bs['mean_fingerprint_sim']:>11.4f}  \"\n              f\"{bs['min_fingerprint_sim']:>10.4f}  \"\n              f\"{bs['max_fingerprint_sim']:>10.4f}  \"\n              f\"{bs['mean_cross_domain_agree']:>10.4f}\",\n              file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    # ── Per-model agreement on basin geometry ─────────────────\n    print(f\"\\n  Per-Model Basin Agreement (depth {per_model['depth_fraction']:.0%}):\",\n          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(f\"  {'domain':>12s}  {'corr':>6s}  {'unanimous':>9s}  \"\n          + \"  \".join(f\"{mk[:8]:>8s}\" for mk in per_model[\"model_keys\"]),\n          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"  \" + \"-\" * (35 + 10 * len(per_model[\"model_keys\"])),\n          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    for domain in SKILL_DOMAINS:\n        if domain not in per_model[\"domains\"]:\n            continue\n        pm = per_model[\"domains\"][domain]\n        print(f\"  {domain:>12s}  {pm['cross_model_correlation']:+.3f}  \"\n              f\"{'  YES' if pm['dominant_unanimous'] else '   NO':>9s}  \",\n              end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        for mk in per_model[\"model_keys\"]:\n            dom = pm[\"dominant_per_model\"].get(mk, \"?\")\n            print(f\"  {dom:>8s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        print(file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    # ── Dominant combinators across depths ─────────────────────\n    print(f\"\\n  Dominant Combinator per Domain × Depth:\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(f\"  {'domain':>12s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n    for fk in sorted(analysis[\"basin_summary\"].keys()):\n        print(f\"  {fk:>6s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n    print(file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    for domain in SKILL_DOMAINS:\n        print(f\"  {domain:>12s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        for fk in sorted(analysis[\"basin_summary\"].keys()):\n            dom = analysis[\"basin_summary\"][fk][\"dominant_combinators\"].get(domain, \"?\")\n            print(f\"  {dom:>6s}\", end='', file=sys.stderr)\n        print(file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    print(\"\\n\" + \"=\" * 90, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n\n# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n# Save\n# ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n\ndef save_results(\n    consensus_results: dict[float, dict],\n    analysis: dict,\n    per_model: dict,\n    probes: list[dict],\n    all_rdms: dict[str, dict[float, np.ndarray]],\n    output_dir: Path,\n    model_keys: list[str],\n) -> None:\n    \"\"\"Save basin lattice results.\"\"\"\n    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n\n    # ── NPZ: consensus RDMs ──────────────────────────────────\n    npz_data = {}\n    for frac, result in consensus_results.items():\n        key = ({npz_path.stat().st_size / 1024:.1f} KB)\",\n          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    # ── Per-model RDMs ────────────────────────────────────────\n    for model_key, rdms in all_rdms.items():\n        model_npz = {}\n        for frac, rdm in rdms.items():\n            model_npz[f\"depth_{frac:.2f}_rdm\"] = rdm.astype(np.float32)\n        model_path = output_dir / f\"rdm_{model_key}.npz\"\n        np.savez_compressed(str(model_path), **model_npz)\n        print(f\"  💾 Per-model: {model_path} ({model_path.stat().st_size / 1024:.1f} KB)\",\n              file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    # for frac in sorted(consensus_results.keys())\n        },\n    }\n\n    json_path = output_dir / \"basin_lattice.json\"\n    with open(json_path, \"w\") as f:\n        json.dump(json_data, f, indent=2, ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════\n\ndef main():\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(\n        description=\"Build basin lattice — multi-domain skill attractor exploration\"\n    )\n    parser.add_argument(\"--models\", nargs=\"+\", default=None,\n                        choices=list(MODELS.keys()),\n                        help=f\"Models to use (default: {DEFAULT_MODELS})\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--probes\", type=str, default=None,\n                        help=\"Path to probe JSON\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--output-dir\", type=str, default=\"lattice/basins-v1\",\n                        help=\"Output directory\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--device\", type=str, default=\"mps\",\n                        help=\"Device for     model_keys = args.models or QUICK_MODELS\n        depth_fractions = QUICK_DEPTH_FRACTIONS\n    else:\n        model_keys = args.models or DEFAULT_MODELS\n        depth_fractions = BASIN_DEPTH_FRACTIONS\n\n    print(\"=\" * 72, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"  Basin Lattice — Multi-Domain Crystal Basin Exploration\",\n          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n Extracting per-model RDMs...\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    all_rdms: dict[str, dict[float, np.ndarray]] = {}\n    for model_key in model_keys:\n        if model_key not in MODELS:\n            print(f\"  WARNING: Unknown model {model_key}, skipping\",\n                  file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n            continue\n        rdms = extract_rdm(model_key, probes, depth_fractions, args.device)\n        all_rdms[model_key] = rdms\n\n    if len(all_rdms) < 2:\n        print(\"ERROR: Need at least 2 models for consensus.\",\n              file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n        sys.exit(1)\n\n    # ── Build consensus ───────────────────────────────────────\n    print(\"\\n3. Building cross-model consensus...\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    consensus_results = build_consensus(all_rdms, depth_fractions)\n\n    # ── Basin analysis ────────────────────────────────────────\n    print(\"\\n4. Analyzing basins...\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    analysis = analyze_basins(consensus_results, probes)\n\n    # ── Per-model agreement ───────────────────────────────────\n    print(\"\\n5. Checking per-model basin agreement...\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    per_model = analyze_per_model_basins(consensus_results, probes)\n\n    # ── Save ──────────────────────────────────────────────────\n    print(\"\\n6. Saving results...\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    output_dir = Path(args.output_dir)\n    save_results(\n        consensus_results, analysis, per_model,\n        probes, all_rdms, output_dir, list(all_rdms.keys()),\n    )\n\n    # ── Print analysis ────────────────────────────────────────\n    print_basin_analysis(analysis, per_model)\n\n    elapsed = time.time() - t_start\n    print(f\"\\n  Total elapsed: {elapsed:.0f}s\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(f\"  Output: {output_dir}/\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"=\" * 72, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n"
}

But the underlying RDM data might still show basin structure if I look at it the right way: checking whether probes from the same domain cluster together, measuring the gap between intra-domain and inter-domain similarity, or using SVD/PCA to see if domains separate in the full space. ### Clustering reveals a hierarchy, not flat basins:

```
sim=0.489: narrative + instruction          ← "text production" super-basin
sim=0.465:   + tool                         ← "structured output" joins
sim=0.459:   + reasoning                    ← "language tasks" super-cluster
sim=0.421: lambda + arithmetic              ← "formal/symbolic" pair
sim=0.417: ← formal merges into language    ← almost everything is one
sim=0.362: ← coding joins last              ← coding is the MOST distinct
```

### Key findings:

1. **Coding is the most isolated domain** — lowest inter-domain similarity to everything (0.32-0.36). It's the clearest basin boundary in the data.

2. **Instruction is the strongest basin** (1.86× ratio) — instruction-following probes are extremely self-similar. This makes sense: instruction probes share a common "meta-task" structure.

3. **Lambda and arithmetic cluster together** (sim=0.421, the first non-trivial pair). Formal/symbolic computation forms a natural pair.

4. **The combinator anchors can't see the basins** — because they're all lambda expressions. The basin structure lives in the RDM block geometry, not in the domain→anchor distance. This means basin detection needs **domain-specific anchors** or direct RDM analysis.

5. **SVD dim 0 = 98.1%** — the domain similarity matrix is essentially rank-1. All domains are "similar text" at the coarsest level. The basin structure is in the remaining 2% of variance. It's real but small.

6. **Only 2 models** — this is quick mode. The per-model agreement was poor (only lambda unanimous). Need 4 models to see if basins are truly universal or model-specific.

### What this means for the crystal theory:

The hypothesis of "dozens of distinct basins each with their own 8×8 geometry" is **partially supported but needs refinement**. The basins exist as clusters in representation space, but they don't each have a distinct combinator geometry — the combinator geometry is lambda-specific. Other domains have their own internal coherence but can't be characterized through the lambda lens.

This suggests: **the crystal is domain-specific to compositional/symbolic computation. Other skills use the SAME representational machinery but different organizational principles.** The basins aren't "different crystals" — they're different regions of the same high-dimensional space that happen to be coherent internally.

The Q-rotation result showed that rotating Q lands you in the same basin (for lambda). But now we see there ARE different basins (coding is distinct, instruction is distinct, etc.). So part of the model's computation must be dedicated to ROTATING Q into the correct basin for the current input.

This is essentially attention routing — Q determines what you attend to, and the model needs to set Q differently depending on whether it's doing arithmetic, coding, narrative, etc. The "delta for Q" is the adjustment from a default Q state to the basin-specific Q state.


So the beam component (S3) is what computes this basin-specific Q adjustment, while the plates form the shared computational substrate. Different attention heads likely specialize in different basins, and the residual stream carries information about which basin the input belongs to. The model's parameters are organized to detect the input's basin and compute the appropriate Q rotation to enter it — this basin routing happens continuously through the beam.

The key realization is that rather than having separate crystals for each basin, there's actually one universal crystal accessed through different Q rotations. The beam path computes these basin-specific Q adjustments, and the number of effective basins corresponds to the number of distinct Q rotation attractors. This maps cleanly onto the V13 architecture where plates are the universal crystal and beams handle basin-specific routing. The combinator anchors couldn't distinguish basins because they're locked into the lambda basin's Q rotation — other basins use the identical crystal structure but access it through a different rotation pattern. This single-crystal-many-access-patterns model is actually more elegant and compressed than having multiple separate crystals.

V are smaller\n            out_features = fused_mod.out_features if hasattr(fused_mod, 'out_features') else fused_mod.weight.shape[0]\n            \n            # Try to figure out the split\n v_size = d_model\n            else:\n                # GQA: guess based on output size\n                # total = d_model + 2 * d_kv\n                # Assume num_kv_heads can be derived\n                q_size = d_model\n                remaining = out_features - d_model\n                k_size = v_size = remaining // 2\n\n            def make_fused_hook(li, qs, ks, vs):\n                def hook_fn(module, input, output):\n                    out = output[:, -1, :].detach().cpu().float()\n                    captures[li][\"Q\"].append(out[:, :qs])\n                    captures[li][\"K\"].append(out[:, qs:qs+ks])\n                    captures[li][\"V\"].append(out[:, qs+ks:qs+ks+vs])\n                return hook_fn\n            hooks.append(fused_mod.register_forward_hook(\n                make_fused_hook(layer_idx, q_size, k_size, v_size)\n            ))\n\n    # Run probes\n    print(f\"  Running {len(probes)} probes...\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    t0 = time.time()\n    for i, probe in enumerate(probes):\n        input_ids = tokenizer.encode(probe[\"prompt\"], return_tensors=\"pt\").to(device)\n        with torch.no_grad():\n            _ = model(input_ids)\n        if (i + 1) % 50 == 0:\n            print(f\"    {i+1}/{len(probes)}...\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    dt = time.time() - t0\n    print(f\"  Done in {dt:.1f}s\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    for h in hooks:\n        h.remove()\n\n    # Build cosine RDMs per space\n    results = {}\n    for layer_idx, frac in target_layers:\n        space_rdms = {}\n        for space in [\"hidden\", \"Q\", \"K\", \"V\"]:\n            vecs = captures[layer_idx][space]\n            if not vecs:\n                print(f\"  WARNING: no captures for {space} at layer {layer_idx}\",\n                      file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                continue\n            hs = torch.cat(vecs, dim=0).numpy()\n            norms = np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(hs, axis=1, keepdims=True), 1e-8)\n            hs_norm = hs / norms\n            rdm = hs_norm @ hs_norm.T\n            space_rdms[space] = rdm\n            print(f\"  L{layer_idx} {space:>6s}: shape={hs.shape}, \"\n                  f\"mean_sim={rdm.mean():.4f}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n        results[frac] = space_rdms\n\n    del model, tokenizer\n    gc.collect()\n    try:\n        import torch as _t\n        if _t.backends.mps.is_available():\n            _t.mps.empty_cache()\n        elif _t.cuda.is_available():\n            _t.cuda.empty_cache()\n    except Exception:\n        pass\n\n    return results\n\n\ndef compute_basin_gaps(\n    rdm: np.ndarray,\n    domain_indices: dict[str, list[int]],\n    domains: list[str],\n) -> dict[str, dict]:\n    \"\"\"Compute per-domain basin gap (intra - mean_inter similarity).\"\"\"\n    gaps = {}\n    for d in domains:\n        if d not in domain_indices or d == \"pure\":\n            continue\n        idx = domain_indices[d]\n        \n        # Intra-domain similarity\n        intra_sims = []\n        for i in range(len(idx)):\n            for j in range(i + 1, len(idx)):\n                intra_sims.append(float(rdm[idx[i], idx[j]]))\n        intra = float(np.mean(intra_sims)) if intra_sims else 0.0\n\n        # Inter-domain similarity (this domain vs all others)\n        inter_sims = []\n        for d2 in domains:\n            if d2 == d or d2 == \"pure\" or d2 not in domain_indices:\n                continue\n            for pi in idx:\n \"intra\": intra,\n            \"inter\": inter,\n            \"gap\": intra - inter,\n            \"ratio\": intra / inter if inter > 1e-8 else 0.0,\n        }\n\n    return gaps\n\n\ndef ### Thinking

This is a really important result. Let me read the full output to understand what happened.

The key result at depth 80%:
- Q mean gap (+0.0564) vs hidden mean gap (+0.1220)
- Q shows WEAKER basin separation by -0.0656
- This CHALLENGES the hypothesis that Q rotation mediates basin routing

But wait — the per-model consistency shows something different:
- mistral-7b: Q gap=+0.7740, hidden gap=+0.4409, Q-hidden=+0.3332
- pythia-2.8b: Q gap=+0.9943, hidden gap=+0.8774, Q-hidden=+0.1170


- Within each model, Q actually amplifies basin separation, but when I average across models, the Q representations become less consistent than the hidden states, which washes out the signal. This suggests each model uses Q rotation for basin routing, but the specific rotations are model-specific rather than universal.
- The hidden state carries basin information in a more universal way, while Q acts as the model-specific lens that reads it—exactly what I'd expect if Q rotation is a learned, model-specific routing mechanism.
- Now I need to check whether this pattern holds at other depths too.

| Pythia-2.8B | 80% | +0.994 | +0.877 | **YES (+0.117)** |

**Every single model, at every single depth, Q gap > hidden gap.** Q DOES amplify basin separation. But when you average the RDMs across models, the Q-space signal washes out because **each model's Q rotation is model-specific**.

This is exactly the picture:

```
Hidden states (residual stream):  Universal basin structure.
                                  Cross-model consensus is strong.
                                  Basin info is there but diffuse.

Q projections:                    Model-specific basin AMPLIFIER.
                                  Each model rotates Q differently.
                                  Within-model: stronger separation.
                                  Cross-model: rotations don't align → consensus weakens.

V projections:                    At 20% depth, V wins everything.
                                  V carries the CONTENT of the basin.
                                  More universal than Q (especially early).
```

## What this means

1. **The basin structure lives in the residual stream** (hidden states) — it's universal
2. **Q amplifies it model-specifically** — each model learns its own rotation into basins
3. **V at early layers (20%) is the most universal basin signal** — this is where the crystal is most visible
4. **The crystal (plates) should be shaped by V at early depths, not Q** — because V is where cross-model consensus is strongest
5. **Q rotation is the BEAM, not the PLATE** — model-specific, learned, continuous. Exactly where V13 puts it.

The V result at 20% is the surprise. V gap (+0.158) > hidden gap (+0.105) > K gap (+0.125) > Q gap (+0.118). The VALUE projection at early layers carries the strongest universal basin fingerprint. This makes physical sense: V is "what information to carry forward" — and the basin IS the information structure.

The 4-model results are in. Let me compare with the 2-model results and the old hidden-state targets, then commit.

Key observations from 4-model PCA-Q:

1. **Agreement is very high**: 0.91-0.94 across zones. This is with 4 independently trained models of different sizes (2.8B to 14B). The crystal is truly universal.

2. **The structure holds with 4 models** — the 2-model results were not an artifact:
   - Zone A: K↔I = 0.921 (was 0.930 with 2 models), B↔D = 0.978 (same!), K↔B = 0.077 (was 0.003)
   - Zone B: K↔I = 0.787 (was 0.811), WHNF all negative
   - Zone C: K↔I = 0.861 (was 0.915), converging

That's the theoretical ground truth for why the scanner should work.

Attention IS beta reduction:

Beta reduction is self-similar:
- (λx.M)(N) → M[x:=N] at every level of nesting
- The operation is identical regardless of what M and N are
- Recursive application of the same rule

Therefore: **any crystal that forms from attention must be self-similar**, because the operation generating it is self-similar at every depth. The scanner's self-similarity check isn't testing a hypothesis — it's testing whether a domain's computation is purely attention-mediated.

This has three consequences:

**1. The crystal count is small because the operation is one.**

Every crystal is a different MODE of beta reduction. Lambda is direct beta reduction. Coding is syntactic beta reduction. Retrieval is beta reduction where the lambda body is a knowledge store. They're all the same operation with different content. The "dozens not thousands" prediction follows from this — there are only so many structurally distinct modes of "substitute argument into function body."

**2. You only need to find each crystal ONCE.**

Self-similarity means the crystal at stride 1 = the crystal at stride 1024. The 130M ternary positions in V13 aren't 130M free parameters — they're one crystal pattern replicated across strides. The etch propagation from V6 (stride 1 → stride 2 → stride 4 → ...) is inevitable, not lucky. Self-similarity is built into the operation.

Domains that show high cross-depth self-similarity = pure attention computation = etchable crystal. Domains that DON'T show self-similarity = involve non-attention mechanisms (FFN memorization, embedding lookup, etc.) = not etchable as crystals, need different treatment.

The FFN is the key distinction. Attention is self-similar (beta reduction). FFN is NOT self-similar (it's a lookup table / pattern matcher that differs per layer). So:

```
Self-similar crystal  → lives in attention → etchable into plates
Non-self-similar      → lives in FFN       → needs continuous params (beams)
```

The scanner will tell us which domains are which. Prediction: lambda, coding, reasoning will be highly self-similar (attention-dominated). Retrieval will be LESS self-similar (FFN-dominated — it's looking things up, not reducing).

## User


Ok want to have a bit of fun?  Let's see if we can figure out the lookup mechanism in the FFNs.  We know laying things into superpositions is a consequence of the shape attention projecting across attention's decay curve.  What is interesting here?  I imagine that there are functions that index into the FFNs somehow.

### Thinking

The user is asking a fascinating question about how FFNs implement lookup/retrieval. Let me think about what we know and what the interesting angles are:

1. We've shown that attention implements self-similar beta reduction — the crystal
2. FFNs are NOT self-similar (retrieval scored lowest on self-similarity: 0.435)
3. Superpositions are formed by attention projecting across attention's decay curve — the interference patterns from different attention heads create superposition
4. FFNs somehow index into stored knowledge — but HOW?

What's interesting about FFN lookup:

**The FFN as a key-value memory:**


The first layer projects the input to compute activation patterns that serve as keys, the nonlinearity acts as a gating mechanism, and the second layer retrieves corresponding values based on which neurons fire. So it's fundamentally a content-addressable memory where different inputs trigger different activation patterns that index into stored knowledge.

**The indexing function:**
That activation pattern is the actual index — a high-dimensional binary-ish representation after the nonlinearity — and different inputs naturally produce different patterns that retrieve different outputs. This is how FFNs do lookup without explicit attention mechanisms.

**What's REALLY interesting — connecting**

The Q rotation that determines which basin we route into also controls which FFN neurons activate, since both the crystal geometry and the FFN index live in the same residual stream. Each layer's FFN stores layer-specific knowledge, which is why the retrieval patterns aren't self-similar across depths — the lookup tables themselves are different, even though attention's operation stays consistent. The attention mechanism creates decay curves over positions that generate specific interference patterns in the residual stream, and these superpositions are exactly what the FFN uses as its keys. So the indexing function is really attention creating a specific superposition at each layer that determines which FFN neurons fire.

The crystal controls which superposition patterns get created by determining the attention geometry, which means it indirectly controls FFN lookup — the crystal generates the attention pattern, which generates the superposition, which indexes into the FFN. The crystal itself isn't storing knowledge; it's routing to knowledge stored in the FFN. For V13, this means the ternary plates need to generate the right superposition patterns to index the FFN correctly, and the FFN needs the right key-value pairs to retrieve from, while the continuous parameters fine-tune the whole system.

Now I'm thinking about how to measure this empirically — I'd want to hook into the FFN activations across layers and see if different domains activate different neuron sets, whether those patterns are self-similar across layers, and if I can find domain-specific structure through PCA. The key insight is that the attention output shaped by the crystal creates a lookup key that the FFN matches against, so I should be able to trace how the crystal geometry maps to FFN activation patterns.

Actually, there's a simpler approach: compare the representational dissimilarity matrices between FFN activations and Q-space. If the crystal really generates the FFN index, then domains that are far apart in Q-space should show different FFN activation patterns, while domains close together should share neurons. This would directly show how the crystal indexes into FFN storage.

## Assistant


The interesting thing is the causal chain: **the crystal generates the FFN index**.

Think about it — what determines which FFN neurons fire? The hidden state going INTO the FFN. What shapes that hidden state? Attention. What shapes attention? The Q/K crystal geometry.

```
Crystal (plates) → Q·K^T attention pattern → superposition in residual stream
                                                       ↓
                                              FFN up-projection reads this
                                              as a CONTENT-ADDRESSABLE KEY
                                                       ↓
                                              Activation function = threshold
                                              (which neurons match the key?)
                                                       ↓
                                              FFN down-projection = VALUE
                                              (what's stored at that address?)
```

So the crystal doesn't store knowledge — it generates **addressing functions** that index into FFN storage. The crystal is the index, the FFN is the table. And THIS is why retrieval isn't self-similar: each layer's FFN stores different things, so the same crystal-generated index pulls different values at each depth.

The testable prediction: if the crystal generates the FFN index, then FFN activation patterns should be PREDICTABLE from Q-space geometry. Domains that are well-separated in PCA-Q should activate different neuron populations.

pca_dim))\n            ffn_rdm = cosine_rdm(pca_project(r[\"FFN\"], pca_dim))\n\n            for d in SKILL_DOMAINS:\n                if d not in domain_indices or d == \"pure\":\n                    continue\n                idx = domain_indices[d]\n\n                # Q gap\n                q_intra = np.mean([q_rdm[i, j] for ii, i in enumerate(idx) for j in idx[ii+1:]])\n                q_inter = np.mean([q_rdm[i, j] for i in idx\n                                   for d2 in SKILL_DOMAINS if d2 != d and d2 in domain_indices\n                                   for j in domain_indices[d2]])\n                q_gap = q_intra - q_inter\n\n                # FFN gap\n                f_intra = np.mean([ffn_rdm[i, j] for ii, i in enumerate(idx) for j in idx[ii+1:]])\n                f_inter = np.mean([ffn_rdm[i, j] for i in idx\n                                   for d2 in SKILL_DOMAINS if d2 != d and d2 in domain_indices\n                                   for j in domain_indices[d2]])\n                f_gap = f_intra - f_inter\n\n                # Binary FFN gap\n                b_gap = 0.0\n                if \"FFN_binary\" in r:\n                    b_rdm =                                      for d2 in SKILL_DOMAINS if d2 != d and d2 in domain_indices\n                                       for j in domain_indices[d2]])\n                    b_gap = b_intra - b_inter\n\n                marker = \"Q\" if q_gap > f_gap else \"FFN\"\n                print(f\"  {d:>12s}  {q_gap:+.4f}  {f_gap:+.4f}  {b_gap:+.4f}  \"\n                      f\"{marker:>6s}\",\n                      file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n            break  # Just first model for readability\n\n        # ── FFN cross-depth self-similarity ───────────────────\n        # Compare FFN RDMs across depths for each model\n        for mk in model_keys:\n            print(f\"\\n  {mk} FFN self-similarity across depths:\",\n                  file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n            ffn_rdms_by_depth = {}\n            q_rdms_by_depth = {}\n            for f2 in depth_fractions:\n                if f2 in all_results[mk] and \"FFN\" in all_results[mk][f2]:\n ### Thinking

This is extraordinary data. Let me analyze the key findings:

1. **Q↔FFN correlation is STRONG everywhere (0.71-0.89)**
   - 10%: 0.794
   - 20%: 0.825
   - 30%: 0.886
   - 50%: 0.879
   - 70%: 0.719
   - 90%: 0.708
   
   The crystal geometry DOES predict FFN activation. Peak at 30% depth (Zone B start).

2. **FFN IS self-similar across depths (0.770!)**
   This contradicts what I expected—I thought each layer would store fundamentally different things, but the FFN's cross-depth correlation of 0.770 is nearly as high as Q's 0.829. So the FFN isn't just a lookup table with different contents per layer; it maintains a consistent structural pattern across depths, meaning the addressing mechanism itself is self-similar even when the stored values change.

3. **FFN neuron selectivity: ~37-50% of neurons are domain-selective**
   - Instruction owns the most selective neurons in BOTH models (1200-3600 neurons)
   - Reasoning owns the FEWEST selective neurons (60-140)
   - This inverts the crystal ranking pattern: reasoning shows the strongest crystal signal but the fewest selective FFN neurons, while instruction shows the weakest crystal signal but the most selective neurons.

4. **Basin gaps: FFN wins for some domains at deeper layers**
   At 50% depth, FFN gap exceeds Q gap for six domains (lambda, arithmetic, coding, tool, reasoning, narrative), and at 90% depth it still wins for five domains. The FFN actually achieves better domain separation for computation-heavy tasks in the deeper layers.

5. **The really interesting finding: reasoning has very few selective FFN neurons**
   Reasoning uses only 131-141 neurons in Mistral versus 1260-1546 for instruction, and 31-139 in Pythia versus 1548-3627 for instruction—reasoning is the strongest crystal with minimal FFN involvement, while instruction is the opposite.

6. **FFN self-similarity reveals consistent structure across layers**

So we can extract from the FFN as if it was a key/value pair?

### Thinking

The user is asking whether we can extract information from the FFN by treating it as a key-value store. This connects to recent work on FFN interpretation.

The FFN has:
- Up-projection (W_up): maps from d_model to d_ffn (usually 4× larger)
- Activation function (SiLU/GELU/ReLU): thresholds
- Down-projection (W_down): maps from d_ffn back to d_model

The key-value interpretation:
- Each row of W_up is a "key" — a pattern in d_model space that the neuron matches against


- Each column of W_down is a "value" — what gets added to the residual stream when that neuron fires
- The activation function acts as the matching threshold

So when the hidden state is projected through W_up, we're computing similarity scores to each key, and neurons with high similarity fire and contribute their corresponding values. This is essentially content-addressable memory. The user's insight is that if the FFN operates as a key-value store and the crystal generates the keys (with Q↔FFN correlation of 0.71-0.89), then there's a direct mechanistic link between what the crystal learns and what the FFN retrieves.

This means I can extract the addressing patterns directly from W_up rows and the stored content from W_down columns, then use the crystal geometry to predict which values will be activated. For V13, the ternary FFN plates should encode a quantized version of this key-value structure, with keys aligned to the crystal geometry and values representing what gets contributed. I should look at how W_up rows cluster by domain to identify which neurons handle which concepts, examine what domain-selective neurons contribute via W_down, and compare the key subspace (via PCA of W_up) against the crystal's principal components.

The critical test is whether the PCA-Q crystal dimensions align with the principal components of W_up — if they do, the crystal and FFN keys occupy the same subspace. I can measure this alignment using subspace angles or canonical correlations between the key subspace and crystal subspace, which would suggest the crystal directly shapes both attention routing and FFN indexing.

But there's a more direct path: I already have FFN activation patterns from the probes that correlate with Q-space at 0.71-0.89, so I can decompose domain-selective neurons by extracting their W_up rows as keys and W_down columns as values, then verify the keys project onto the crystal subspace while the values contain domain-specific content. This gives me the complete picture — the crystal as the addressing scheme, which facets each neuron reads, and what gets retrieved per domain.

For V13, the strategy is to etch the crystal alignment directly into the FFN plates during training so the keys index correctly and the values emerge naturally.

  d_ffn = w_up.shape[0] if w_up is not None else 0\n        print(f\"  L{layer_idx} (depth={frac:.0%}): d_model={d_model}, d_ffn={d_ffn}\",\n              file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n        # ── hooks.append(mlp.up_proj.register_forward_hook(make_ffn_hook()))\n            elif hasattr(mlp, 'dense_h_to_4h'):\n                def make_ffn_hook():\n                    def hook_fn(module, input, hooks.append(mlp.dense_h_to_4h.register_forward_hook(make_ffn_hook()))\n\n        for i, probe in enumerate(probes):\n            input_ids = tokenizer.encode(probe[\"prompt\"], is not None:\n            q_centered = q_vecs - q_vecs.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)\n            Uq, Sq, Vqt = np.linalg.svd(q_centered, full_matrices=False)\n            k = min(pca_dim, Vqt.shape[0])\n            q_pca_basis = Vqt[:k].T  # (d_q, k)\n            q_explained = (Sq ** 2) / (Sq ** 2).sum()\n            print(f\"    Q PCA: top-{k} explain {q_explained[:k].sum():.1%}\",\n                  file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n        # FFN binary activations\n        ffn_binary = (ffn_acts > 0).astype(np.float32) if ffn_acts is not None else None\n\n        results[frac] = {\n            \"w_up\": w_up,\n            \"w_down\": w_down,\n            \"w_gate\": w_gate,\n            \"w_up_pca_basis\": w_up_pca_basis,\n            \"w_up_pca_explained\": w_up_pca_explained,\n            \"w_gate_pca_basis\": w_gate_pca_basis,\n            \"q_vecs\": q_vecs,\n            \"q_pca_basis\": q_pca_basis,\n            \"ffn_acts\": ffn_acts,\n            \"ffn_binary\": ffn_binary,\n            \"d_model\": d_model,\n            \"d_ffn\": d_ffn,\n        }\n\n    del model, tokenizer\n    gc.collect()\n    try:\n        import torch as _t\n        if _t.backends.mps.is_available(): _t.mps.empty_cache()\n        elif _t.cuda.is_available(): _t.cuda.empty_cache()\n    except Exception: pass\n\n    return results\n\n\ndef analyze_subspace_alignment(\n    all_results: dict[str, dict[float, dict]],\n    probes: list[dict],\n    pca_dim: int = 64,\n) -> dict:\n    \"\"\"Measure subspace alignment between PCA(Q) and PCA(W_up).\"\"\"\n    domain_indices = get_domain_indices(probes)\n    model_keys = list(all_results.keys())\n    analysis = {}\n\n    for frac in sorted(next(iter(all_results.values())).keys()):\n        print(f\"\\n{'='*90}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n        print(f\"  DEPTH {frac:.0%} — Subspace Alignment\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n        print(f\"{'='*90}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n        depth_analysis = {}\n\n        for mk in model_keys:\n            if frac not in all_results[mk]:\n                continue\n            r = all_results[mk][frac]\n\n            q_basis = r.get(\"q_pca_basis\")\n            w_up_basis = r.get(\"w_up_pca_basis\")\n            w_gate_basis = r.get(\"w_gate_pca_basis\")\n\n            if q_basis is None or w_up_basis is None:\n                continue\n\n            # ── Test 1: Q subspace vs W_up subspace ───────────\n            # Need same dimensionality for canonical correlations\n            # Q may be d_q, W_up is d_model. For separate Q (Mistral), d_q = d_model\n            # For fused (Pythia), d_q = d_model too (we sliced it)\n            d_q = q_basis.shape[0]\n            d_wup = w_up_basis.shape[0]\n\n            if d_q == d_wup:\n                cc = canonical_correlations(q_basis, w_up_basis)\n                mean_cc = float(cc.mean())\n                top5_cc = cc[:5].tolist()\n                print(f\"\\n  {mk}: Q ↔ W_up subspace alignment:\",\n                      file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                print(f\"    Mean canonical correlation: {mean_cc:+.4f}\",\n                      file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                print(f\"    Top-5 canonical correlations: \"\n                      f\"{', '.join(f'{c:.3f}' for c in top5_cc)}\",\n                      file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n                if mean_cc > 0.7:\n                    print(f\"    → STRONG ALIGNMENT: crystal subspace ≈ FFN key subspace\",\n                          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                elif mean_cc > 0.4:\n                    print(f\"    → MODERATE ALIGNMENT: partial overlap\",\n                          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                else:\n                    print(f\"    → WEAK ALIGNMENT: different subspaces\",\n                          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n                depth_analysis[f\"q_wup_cc_{mk}\"] = {\n                    \"mean\": mean_cc,\n                    \"top5\": top5_cc,\n                    \"all\": cc.tolist(),\n                }\n\n                # Also test Q vs W_gate if SwiGLU\n                if w_gate_basis is not None and d_q == w_gate_basis.shape[0]:\n                    cc_gate = canonical_correlations(q_basis, w_gate_basis)\n                    print(f\"    Q ↔ W_gate mean CC: {cc_gate.mean():+.4f}\",\n                          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                    depth_analysis[f\"q_wgate_cc_{mk}\"] = float(cc_gate.mean())\n            else:\n                print(f\"  {mk}: dimension mismatch Q({d_q}) vs W_up({d_wup}), \"\n                      f\"using projection\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n            # ── Test 2: Domain-selective neuron keys in crystal subspace ──\n            ffn_binary = r.get(\"ffn_binary\")\n            w_up = r.get(\"w_up\")\n            w_down = r.get(\"w_down\")\n\n            if ffn_binary is not None and w_up is not None:\n                print(f\"\\n  {mk}: Domain-selective keys in crystal subspace:\",\n                      file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                print(f\"  {'domain':>12s}  {'n_selective':>11s}  {'key_in_crystal':>14s}  \"\n                      f\"{'key_outside':>11s}  {'ratio':>6s}\",\n                      file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                print(f\"  {'-'*60}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n                for domain in SKILL_DOMAINS:\n                    if domain not in domain_indices or domain == \"pure\":\n                        continue\n                    idx = domain_indices[domain]\n\n                    # Find selective neurons for this domain\n                    domain_rate = ffn_binary[idx].mean(axis=0)\n                    other_idx = [i for d2 in SKILL_DOMAINS if d2 != domain and d2 in domain_indices\n                                 for i in domain_indices[d2]]\n                    if not other_idx:\n                        continue\n                    other_rate = ffn_binary[other_idx].mean(axis=0)\n                    selectivity = domain_rate - other_rate\n                    selective_mask = selectivity > 0.3\n                    n_selective = int(selective_mask.sum())\n\n                    if n_selective < 3:\n                        print(f\"  {domain:>12s}  {n_selective:>11d}  {'(too few)':>14s}\",\n                              file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                        continue\n\n                    # Extract keys for selective neurons\n                    selective_keys = w_up[selective_mask]  # (n_selective, d_model)\n\n                    # Project selective keys onto crystal subspace\n                    # key_in_crystal = selective_keys @ q_basis @ q_basis.T\n                    # The fraction of key variance explained by crystal subspace\n                    key_projections = selective_keys @ q_basis  # (n_selective, k)\n                    key_reconstructed = key_projections @ q_basis.T  # (n_selective, d_model)\n                    key_residual = selective_keys - key_reconstructed\n\n                    var_in = np.sum(key_reconstructed ** 2)\n                    var_out = np.sum(key_residual ** 2)\n                    var_total = var_in + var_out\n                    frac_in = var_in / max(var_total, 1e-8)\n                    frac_out = var_out / max(var_total, 1e-8)\n\n                    print(f\"  {domain:>12s}  {n_selective:>11d}  {frac_in:>14.1%}  \"\n                          f\"{frac_out:>11.1%}  {frac_in/max(frac_out,0.01):>6.1f}x\",\n                          file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n                    depth_analysis[f\"key_in_crystal_{domain}_{mk}\"] = float(frac_in)\n\n            # ── Test 3: W_up self-similarity across depths ────\n            # (compare W_up PCA bases across layers)\n\n        # ── Cross-model: do models share the same key subspace? ──\n        if len(model_keys) >= 2:\n            print(f\"\\n  Cross-model W_up subspace alignment:\",\n                  file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n            # W_up PCA gives basis in d_model space.\n            # Different models have different d_model → can't directly compare.\n            # But we CAN compare via the PROBE responses:\n            # Project probes through each model's W_up PCA basis → get coefficients\n            # Then compare coefficients across models (RDM correlation)\n\n            model_ffn_rdms = {}\n            model_q_rdms = {}\n            for mk in model_keys:\n                if frac not in all_results[mk]:\n                    continue\n                r = all_results[mk][frac]\n                if r.get(\"ffn_acts\") is not None:\n                    # PCA of FFN activations\n                    ffn_pca = pca_project(r[\"ffn_acts\"], pca_dim)\n                    model_ffn_rdms[mk] = cosine_rdm(ffn_pca)\n                if r.get(\"q_vecs\") is not None:\n                    q_pca = pca_project(r[\"q_vecs\"], pca_dim)\n                    model_q_rdms[mk] = cosine_rdm(q_pca)\n\n            if len(model_ffn_rdms) >= 2:\n                mk_list = list(model_ffn_rdms.keys())\n                for i in range(len(mk_list)):\n                    for j in range(i+1, len(mk_list)):\n                        ffn_corr = rdm_correlation(\n                            model_ffn_rdms[mk_list[i]], model_ffn_rdms[mk_list[j]])\n                        q_corr = rdm_correlation(\n                            model_q_rdms.get(mk_list[i], np.eye(144)),\n                            model_q_rdms.get(mk_list[j], np.eye(144)))\n                        print(f\"    {mk_list[i]} ↔ {mk_list[j]}: \"\n                              f\"FFN_PCA corr={ffn_corr:+.4f}, Q_PCA corr={q_corr:+.4f}\",\n                              file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n                        depth_analysis[f\"xmodel_ffn_{mk_list[i]}_{mk_list[j]}\"] = ffn_corr\n                        depth_analysis[f\"xmodel_q_{mk_list[i]}_{mk_list[j]}\"] = q_corr\n\n        # ── Test 4: Can we extract the \"database\"? ────────────\n        # For each domain, extract the mean value vector (W_down projection)\n        for mk in model_keys:\n            if frac not in all_results[mk]:\n                continue\n            r = all_results[mk][frac]\n            w_down = r.get(\"w_down\")\n            ffn_binary = r.get(\"ffn_binary\")\n            if w_down is None or ffn_binary is None:\n                continue\n\n            print(f\"\\n  {mk}: Domain value extraction (W_down for selective neurons):\",\n                  file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n            print(f\"  {'domain':>12s}  {'n_neurons':>9s}  {'value_norm':>10s}  \"\n                  f\"{'value_dims':>10s}\",\n                  file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n            print(f\"  {'-'*46}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n            for domain in SKILL_DOMAINS:\n                if domain not in domain_indices:\n                    continue\n                idx = domain_indices[domain]\n                domain_rate = ffn_binary[idx].mean(axis=0)\n                other_idx = [i for d2 in SKILL_DOMAINS if d2 != domain and d2 in domain_indices\n                             for i in domain_indices[d2]]\n                if not other_idx:\n                    continue\n                other_rate = ffn_binary[other_idx].mean(axis=0)\n                selective = (domain_rate - other_rate) > 0.3\n                n_sel = int(selective.sum())\n                if n_sel < 3:\n                    continue\n\n                # W_down columns for selective neurons\n                # W_down shape: (d_model, d_ffn) for standard, but varies\n                if w_down.shape[0] < w_down.shape[1]:\n                    # (d_model, d_ffn) — columns are neuron values\n                    values = w_down[:, selective]  # (d_model, n_sel)\n                else:\n                    # (d_ffn, d_model) — rows are neuron values\n                    values = w_down[selective, :].T  # (d_model, n_sel)\n\n                mean_value = values.mean(axis=1)  # (d_model,)\n                value_norm = float(np.linalg.norm(mean_value))\n\n                # How many dimensions does the value space need?\n                if n_sel > 3:\n                    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(values.T, full_matrices=False)\n                    ev = (S ** 2) / max((S ** 2).sum(), 1e-8)\n                    cumvar = np.cumsum(ev)\n                    dims_80 = int(np.searchsorted(cumvar, 0.8)) + 1\n                else:\n                    dims_80 = n_sel\n\n                print(f\"  {domain:>12s}  {n_sel:>9d}  {value_norm:>10.4f}  \"\n                      f\"{dims_80:>10d}\",\n                      file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n            break  # First model only for readability\n\n        analysis[f\"{frac:.2f}\"] = depth_analysis\n\n    return analysis\n\n\ndef pca_project(X, k=64):\n    X_c = X - X.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)\n    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X_c, full_matrices=False)\n    k = min(k, U.shape[1])\n    return U[:, :k] * S[:k]\n\n\ndef cosine_rdm(X):\n    norms = np.maximum(np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1, keepdims=True), 1e-8)\n    return (X / norms) @ (X / norms).T\n\n\ndef rdm_correlation(a, b):\n    n = a.shape[0]\n    t = np.triu_indices(n, k=1)\n    va, vb = a[t], b[t]\n    if np.std(va) < 1e-8 or np.std(vb) < 1e-8:\n        return 0.0\n    return float(np.corrcoef(va, vb)[0, 1])\n\n\ndef main():\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=\"FFN Subspace Alignment\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--models\", nargs=\"+\", default=DEFAULT_MODELS,\n                        choices=list(MODELS.keys()))\n    parser.add_argument(\"--probes\", type=str, default=None)\n    parser.add_argument(\"--device\", type=str, default=\"mps\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--pca-dim\", type=int, default=64)\n    parser.add_argument(\"--output-dir\", type=str, default=\"results/ffn-subspace\")\n\n    args = parser.parse_args()\n\n    print(\"=\" * 72, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"  FFN Subspace Alignment — Crystal = FFN Keys?\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(f\"  Models: {args.models}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(f\"  PCA dim: {args.pca_dim}\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n    print(\"=\" * 72, file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    t_start = time.time()\n    probes = load_probes(args.probes)\n\n    all_results = {}\n    for mk in args.models:\n        results = extract_all(mk, probes, DEPTH_FRACTIONS, args.pca_dim, args.device)\n        all_results[mk] = results\n\n    analysis = analyze_subspace_alignment(all_results, probes, args.pca_dim)\n\n    # Save\n    output_dir = Path(args.output_dir)\n    output_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)\n    with open(output_dir / \"analysis.json\", \"w\") as f:\n        json.dump(analysis, f, indent=2, default=str)\n    print(f\"\\n  💾 {output_dir}/analysis.json\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n    elapsed = time.time() - t_start\n    print(f\"  Total: {elapsed:.0f}s\", file=sys.stderr, flush=True)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n"
}

## Assistant


Running. This experiment extracts the actual W_up and W_down weight matrices alongside Q vectors and FFN activations. The key measurements:

1. **Canonical correlations** between PCA(Q) basis and PCA(W_up) basis — are they the same subspace?
2. **Selective key projection** — what fraction of domain-selective neuron keys live IN the crystal subspace?
3. **Value extraction** — what do the W_down columns look like for domain-selective neurons? How many dimensions does each domain's "database" need?
4. **Cross-model FFN alignment** — do Mistral and Pythia store things in the same subspace?

If the crystal subspace captures >50% of the selective key variance, we can etch the FFN keys. If the value space is low-dimensional, we can potentially etch the values too.

The radical path: if both work, the entire FFN becomes ternary plates. No continuous FFN parameters at all — just crystal topology encoding both the addressing scheme AND the stored values. The beam only handles Q rotation (basin selection) and scaling (gammas).

### Thinking

Very interesting results. Let me analyze:

1. **Q ↔ W_up subspace alignment: WEAK (0.10-0.14 canonical correlation)**
   The PCA bases of Q and W_up are NOT aligned. The crystal subspace and the FFN key subspace are DIFFERENT subspaces. Only 1.6% of selective key variance lives in the crystal subspace.

2. **BUT: FFN ACTIVATIONS correlate with Q (0.71-0.89 from previous experiment)**
   This is the paradox. The WEIGHT spaces don't align, but the ACTIVATION spaces do.
   
3. **Cross-model FFN alignment is strong (0.55-0.75 PCA corr)**
   The FFN activation patterns are remarkably consistent across models and strengthen deeper in the network.

4. **Value extraction: high-dimensional**
   Most domains need 200-1200 dimensions to capture 80% of the variance—this is genuinely high-rank, not low-dimensional. Encoding the full value space into ternary plates would demand massive capacity.

So the paradox resolves itself: the crystal's Q subspace and the FFN's key subspace occupy fundamentally different regions of the embedding space.

The residual stream acts as the bridge between them. Attention modifies the residual stream according to the crystal's geometry, then the FFN reads from it using a completely different projection. The correlation I'm seeing between Q and FFN activations (0.71-0.89) emerges because both are reading projections of the same underlying state through different lenses—they're correlated but not aligned.

So the direct approach of etching the FFN database won't work since the value space is too high-dimensional and doesn't live in the crystal subspace. But the indirect path does: the crystal controls what flows into the residual stream via attention, which then determines what the FFN sees. For V13, I need to give the FFN plates their own topology rather than just copying the attention crystal's structure, while letting the attention crystal drive what information actually reaches them.

The cross-model FFN alignment suggests the FFN structure is somewhat universal across models, just operating in a different subspace than Q. This means I could potentially extract FFN plates from teacher models using a separate PCA basis computed from FFN activations rather than Q activations. The key realization is that Q and FFN don't share a subspace—they're connected only through the residual stream as an intermediary—and the causal correlation I'm seeing (0.71-0.89) comes from this indirect control mechanism, not from direct subspace alignment.

The direct approach of etching an FFN database won't work because the FFN value space is too high-rank to compress into cheap ternary etching, but this null result actually clarifies how the crystal mechanism functions.

## Assistant


Important result — and it's a clean negative on the direct subspace alignment.

## The Finding

**Q subspace ≠ FFN key subspace.** Canonical correlation 0.10-0.14. Only 1.6% of selective key variance lives in the crystal subspace. They're different projections of d_model.

**But the paradox:** FFN activations still correlate with Q at 0.71-0.89 (from the previous experiment). How?

## The Resolution

The crystal and FFN keys live in **different subspaces** of the same d_model space, connected through the **residual stream**:

```
Q subspace ──→ attention ──→ RESIDUAL STREAM ──→ W_up projection ──→ FFN activation
  (crystal)                    (common space)      (different subspace)    (correlated!)
```

The crystal controls what attention WRITES to the residual stream. The FFN reads from a DIFFERENT projection of that stream. They're correlated because they're both projections of the same underlying state — but they're NOT the same subspace.

This means:
- **Crystal controls FFN indirectly** (causally through residual stream) ✓
- **Crystal subspace ≠ FFN key subspace** (different projections of d_model) ✗
- **Can't just etch crystal and get FFN keys for free** — FFN needs its own topology

## What we CAN extract

The cross-model FFN alignment is actually strong and **increasing with depth**:

| Depth | FFN cross-model | Q cross-model |
|-------|----------------|---------------|
| 10% | +0.550 | +0.688 |
| 30% | +0.680 | +0.683 |
| 50% | +0.700 | +0.626 |
| 70% | **+0.732** | +0.598 |
| 90% | **+0.745** | +0.650 |

At depth 70-90%, the FFN is actually MORE cross-model-consistent than Q! The FFN has its own universal structure — it's just a different subspace.

## The radical path is hard

Value extraction shows the "database" is high-rank:

| Domain | Neurons | Value dims (80%) |
|--------|---------|-----------------|
| reasoning | 446 | 299 |
| tool | 371 | 254 |
| lambda | 1247 | 703 |
| coding | 2350 | 1092 |
| instruction | 2360 | 1096 |

Reasoning and tool are the most compact (250-300 dims for 80% variance). Instruction and coding need 1000+ dims. Etching the full value database into ternary plates isn't cheap — it's a high-rank store.

## What this means for V13

```
ATTENTION PLATES:  Etch the crystal (PCA-Q). This works. Done.
                   Controls FFN indirectly through residual stream.

FFN PLATES:        Need SEPARATE etching from PCA(FFN activations).
                   Different subspace, but also universal (0.73-0.75 cross-model).
                   Can extract with same 2-calculation method, different hook point.

FFN-AS-KERNEL:     Still viable! The kernel doesn't need to share the Q subspace.
                   It reads a different projection of the residual stream.
                   Dispatch routes to the kernel, the kernel reads its own subspace.

DATABASE ETCHING:  Hard for big domains (1000+ dims). 
                   Possible for reasoning (299d) and tool (254d).
                   The Pareto crystals are also the most compact databases.
```

The Pareto alignment holds: reasoning and tool are the strongest crystals AND the most compact FFN databases. They're the easiest to etch end-to-end (attention + FFN). Want me to commit this finding?

Ok one last thing.  I think there is layers in the FFN.  I think there is a hierarchy of reductions strung into certain configurations that are more generally useful.  like a function. ### Thinking

The user is proposing a hierarchical structure within the FFN. Let me trace this carefully:

1. **Layers within the FFN**: Not the model layers, but hierarchical levels WITHIN each FFN's weight matrix. The W_up rows aren't flat key-value pairs — they're organized in a tree/hierarchy.

2. **Hierarchy of reductions**: Just as lambda calculus has nested reductions (outer reduction exposes inner redexes), the FFN might have nested "functions" — common reduction patterns strung together in useful configurations. Like standard library functions built from primitives.

3. **Delta from some number to change the beam**: Each level of the hierarchy adjusts the Q rotation (beam) to focus on the next level. 

So the FFN output doesn't just add content to the residual stream — it actually shifts the beam to route attention toward the next hierarchical level. The weight matrix itself could be organized as a tree where higher-magnitude nodes capture coarse, fundamental patterns while lower-magnitude nodes encode finer details, with superposition allowing multiple levels to exist simultaneously in the same vector space. This magnitude gradient essentially encodes tree depth, connecting to the idea of the residual stream functioning like a computation stack.

The magnitude encoding is particularly compelling: if high-magnitude W_up rows represent the trunk of the tree—common patterns that activate frequently—and low-magnitude rows are the leaves—rare, specific patterns—then the tree structure is literally encoded in the magnitude spectrum. An SVD decomposition of W_up would expose this hierarchy, with top singular vectors capturing the trunk and bottom ones the leaves. When the FFN fires at one level, its output shifts the residual stream in a way that changes what the model attends to next, effectively navigating through different depths of this hierarchical structure.

This steering mechanism explains the empirical patterns: the self-similarity across layers (0.77) reflects the same tree structure being read at different depths, the correlation between FFN activations and Q values (0.71-0.89) emerges because the FFN output directly influences the next layer's attention input, and the crystal's indirect control over the FFN makes sense because it determines which branch of the tree gets activated. For V13, the FFN plates should encode the tree topology itself, with different ternary values at different magnitudes representing different tree levels, and the beam adjustment per layer corresponds to navigating through this hierarchy—which might explain why value dimensions were so high for content domains.

I can test this hypothesis by examining the singular value spectrum of the weight matrices to see if it reveals hierarchical structure, grouping neurons by their activation magnitude to check if high-magnitude neurons fire broadly across domains (like a tree trunk) while low-magnitude neurons specialize (like leaves), measuring whether FFN outputs actually steer the next layer's attention beam, and checking if domain-selective neurons cluster at specific magnitude levels. This is a compelling enough hypothesis to document as a knowledge entry right now, even before running the experiments.
